newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa may make legal challenge to SmithKline.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa may make legal challenge to SmithKline.

text.p: South Africa's health ministry said on Thursday it was likely to challenge Anglo-American drug company SmithKline Beecham Plc in court over the firm's attempts to overturn proposed reforms.
SmithKline is taking legal action to scrap plans by health minister Nkosazana Zuma which would make prescribing generic drugs mandatory by medical practitioners in the public health system.

Zuma also plans to allow only, as yet undefined, licensed persons to be able to dispense medicines. The industry fears that may rule out many currently dispensing medical practitioners, such as dentists.
The plans have caused outrage in the South African drugs industry.
Generic drugs are cheaper versions of branded products that have come off patent.
The firm has filed a submission asking the Supreme Court's Transvaal Division to fight the regulation, called R1150, which is part of an overall reform programme for healthcare in South Africa.
"There is a very strong likelihood that we will challenge it (the submission)," said health ministry spokesman Vincent Hlongwane.
But Hlongwane added that the ministry would consult its legal advisors over the next few days before making a final decision on whether or not to enter the courts.
"We are going to get advice from our lawyers...within a few days we will make our position clear," Hlongwane said. The ministry has to make its decision by the end of next week.
SmithKline says moves to limit the use of branded drugs denies doctors choice and could force them to change established patient regimes.
SmithKline South Africa chief executive Gunter Faber said the firm had not had any official contact with the health ministry since news of the spat broke late in September.
"There have been no discussions at all," he said.
Faber declined to discuss the situation further as the case was sub judice.
But a company source said the firm was confident of success and had received some indications that the government may not challenge SmithKline's submission.
"We are fairly confident...we think the advice they (the ministry) have had up front is that they were making a mistake," the source said.

If the two sides do end up settling their diferences in court it will be the latest in a series of battles between the health ministry and the drugs industry that have seen insults traded by both parties.
Relations have sunk so low that some industry executives have warned international firms may be discouraged from investing in South Africa.
In September the head of the South African arm of German drugs group Boehringer Mannheim warned foreign firms may pull out.
"If an industry is not welcome in a country, then companies have to think about down-sizing of operations and moving into a more friendly environment," chief executive Knut Seifert said.
